pages.body:
In many rural communities in Ghana, especially in forest and savanna zones, land is plentiful but fertilisers are expensive or unavailable. Traditional farmers have developed clever systems to keep their soil productive without buying chemical inputs. Two of the oldest are shifting cultivation and land rotation, which are often confused with each other because both involve leaving land to rest.

- What do you think happens to the soil when a farmer grows crops on the same land every season without a rest?
- Can you think of any difference between a farmer who moves completely to new land and one who rotates between fixed plots?

pages.title: Shifting Cultivation
pages.body: Shifting cultivation is a farming system in which a farmer clears new land, usually by cutting down vegetation and burning it (slash-and-burn), grows crops on that land for two to three seasons, and then permanently abandons it and moves on to clear entirely new land elsewhere. The abandoned land is left to regenerate naturally over many years, but the farmer does not plan to return to it systematically. This system is associated with forest zones and is traditional to many indigenous farming communities. It requires large areas of available land and involves a semi-nomadic lifestyle.

**Merits (advantages)**
- No cost of fertilisers; the natural vegetation provides nutrients through ash after burning.
- Effective pest and disease control through moving away from infested land.
- Well adapted to areas with very low population density and abundant land.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Leads to deforestation and destruction of ecosystems as new land is continuously cleared.
- Not sustainable in densely populated areas where land is scarce.
- Produces greenhouse gases when vegetation is burned, contributing to climate change.
- Soil erosion is common after land is abandoned without cover.

pages.title: Land Rotation
pages.body: Land rotation is a more organised system in which a farmer has several defined plots of land and cultivates them in a planned rotation. While one plot is actively farmed, the other plots are left fallow (resting) so that natural vegetation can grow back and restore soil fertility. After a set period, the farmer moves to the next plot, allowing the previously farmed plot to rest. Unlike shifting cultivation, the farmer does not clear new land or change location. The same plots are revisited repeatedly in the rotation cycle. This system is practised in northern and other areas of Ghana where land is moderately available.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Soil fertility is restored naturally during the fallow period.
- The farmer stays in one area and has a stable base.
- Low cost of fertilisers, as resting land replenishes naturally.
- Reduces pest and disease build-up by allowing land to regenerate.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Requires more land than a single continuously cultivated plot.
- During fallow periods, land that could produce food is idle.
- As population grows and land becomes scarcer, there may not be enough land for a full rotation cycle.
- Does not restore soil as quickly as commercial fertilisers.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Shifting Cultivation vs Land Rotation: a critical comparison

pages.title: Shifting Cultivation vs Land Rotation: a critical comparison
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Shifting Cultivation** | **Land Rotation** |
|---|---|---|
| Does the farmer move permanently? | Yes. The farmer abandons old land and clears entirely new land. | No. The farmer stays in the same location and returns to rested plots. |
| Is the land planned and defined? | No. New land is cleared as needed with no fixed rotation plan. | Yes. The farmer has specific, defined plots that are cycled systematically. |
| Main method of clearing land | Slash-and-burn (cutting + burning vegetation on new land). | No new clearing; existing plots are simply left to regenerate. |
| Environmental impact | Higher. Continuous forest clearing destroys habitats. | Lower. No new land is cleared. |
| Land area needed | Very large (always moving to new areas). | Moderate (several plots but in one location). |
| Population density it suits | Very low (abundant, uninhabited land needed). | Low to moderate. |

> **Did you know?** Shifting cultivation was sustainable for thousands of years when human populations were small and forests were vast. Today, with Ghana's growing population and shrinking forest cover, shifting cultivation is increasingly problematic and contributes to deforestation.

questions.q: Define shifting cultivation and land rotation in your own words.
State two ways in which shifting cultivation and land rotation are similar.
State three ways in which they are different.
Explain why shifting cultivation is becoming less practical in Ghana today.

pages.body:
A maize farmer plants maize on the same land every single year. His neighbour plants maize this year, cowpeas next year, and yam the year after, then returns to maize. A large plantation 10 km away grows only cocoa across hundreds of hectares.

- Which farmer do you think will have fewer pest problems over time? Why?
- What do you think is the difference between planting only one crop on a small farm versus on a huge plantation?

pages.title: Crop Rotation
pages.body:
Crop rotation is a farming system in which different crops are grown on the same piece of land in a planned sequence over successive seasons. The sequence is designed so that each crop improves or maintains the soil condition for the next. Crop rotation is practised on the same land without the farmer needing to move, and it keeps the land productive throughout the year.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Restores soil fertility naturally, especially when leguminous crops are included in the rotation.
- Breaks the life cycles of pests and diseases specific to one crop.
- Reduces the need to purchase chemical fertilisers.
- Keeps the land productive throughout the year with different harvests.
- Reduces soil erosion by keeping the land covered for longer.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Requires careful planning and knowledge of which crops complement each other.
- Some crops in the rotation may have lower market demand.
- Farmer must have markets for all crops in the rotation, not just the most popular.
- Income is spread across different crops rather than concentrated in one high-value crop.

pages.title: Principles of crop rotation
pages.body:
Crop rotation is not random. It follows specific principles to be effective.

| **Principle** | **Explanation** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Include a legume | Leguminous crops have bacteria in their roots that fix nitrogen gas from the air into the soil, naturally restoring one of the most important plant nutrients. | Cowpeas, groundnuts, soybeans or beans should appear in every rotation cycle. |
| Alternate deep-rooted and shallow-rooted crops | Deep-rooted crops access nutrients and water from deep in the soil. Shallow-rooted crops use the upper layers. Alternating them avoids exhausting any one depth. | Yam (deep roots) alternated with maize (shallow roots). |
| Never plant the same crop family twice in a row | Crops in the same plant family share the same pests and diseases. Growing them in sequence allows pests to persist and multiply. | Do not follow maize with sorghum (both are grasses). Follow maize with cowpeas instead. |
| Follow heavy feeders with light feeders | Some crops (heavy feeders) remove large amounts of nutrients from the soil. They should be followed by light feeders that demand less. | Maize (heavy feeder) followed by cowpeas (light feeder and nitrogen fixer). |
| Plan for continuous ground cover | The land should not be left bare between crops, to prevent soil erosion and weed growth. | Overlap planting times so one crop is growing while another is being harvested. |

pages.title: Monocropping
pages.body:
Monocropping is a farming system in which only one crop is grown on a piece of land during one growing season. The following season, a different crop may be planted. This is different from monoculture (see below) because monocropping allows crop changes between seasons. It is common among smallholder farmers who plant one crop at a time on each plot and may change what they plant each year based on market prices or availability of seeds.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Simpler to manage than growing multiple crops simultaneously.
- Easier to apply specific fertilisers, pesticides or machinery suited to one crop.
- The farmer can focus all effort on maximising the yield of one crop.
- Easier to harvest when only one crop is ready at the same time.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- If the single crop fails due to drought, pests or disease, the farmer has no other harvest to fall back on.
- Does not use land as efficiently as mixed cropping or crop rotation.
- If practised on the same crop every season, it depletes specific soil nutrients.
- Offers less income diversity than mixed cropping.

pages.title: Monoculture
pages.body:
Monoculture is a farming system in which the same single crop species is grown on a large area of land season after season, year after year. Unlike monocropping, monoculture involves the same crop repeatedly over many years with no rotation. It is most associated with large commercial plantations. In Ghana, examples include cocoa plantations, rubber plantations, oil palm estates and pineapple farms for export.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Highly efficient for large-scale mechanised production.
- Easier to apply uniform inputs (fertilisers, pesticides) across a large area.
- Produces large volumes of a single product, which simplifies marketing and export.
- Workers and machinery become highly specialised and efficient.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Rapidly exhausts specific soil nutrients because the same crop removes the same elements every year.
- Creates ideal conditions for pests and diseases to build up and spread rapidly over the entire crop.
- Heavy dependence on chemical fertilisers and pesticides, increasing costs and environmental impact.
- Total crop failure in any season affects the entire farm income.
- Reduces biodiversity as natural habitat is replaced by a single species.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Crop Rotation vs Monocropping vs Monoculture: a comparison

pages.title: Crop Rotation vs Monocropping vs Monoculture: a comparison
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Crop Rotation** | **Monocropping** | **Monoculture** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Same crop every season? | No. Different crops in a planned sequence. | Not necessarily. Crop may change each season. | Yes. Same crop year after year. |
| Scale | Usually small to medium farms. | Small to medium farms. | Usually large commercial farms. |
| Soil fertility management | Built into the system through legumes and diverse crops. | Depends on fertiliser application. | Relies heavily on chemical fertilisers. |
| Pest/disease risk | Low. Rotation breaks pest cycles. | Moderate. | High. Pests build up rapidly. |
| Income diversity | Moderate. Multiple crops harvested. | Moderate. One crop per season but may vary. | Low. One crop only. |

questions.q: State five principles of crop rotation and explain each one.
Explain the difference between monocropping and monoculture.
Why is monoculture associated with high pest and disease risk?
Design a three-season crop rotation plan for a small Ghanaian farm using local crops. State which crops you would grow in each season and explain why you chose that order.

pages.body:
Consider these three farms. Farm A grows maize and cassava on the same plot at the same time. Farm B grows maize and also keeps goats; the goat droppings are used as manure on the maize. Farm C keeps cattle, sheep and goats across large open grasslands and grows no crops at all.

- How are Farm A and Farm B similar? How are they different?
- What advantage does Farm B have over Farm A?
- What kind of land and climate do you think would suit Farm C best?

pages.title: Mixed Cropping (Intercropping)
pages.body:
Mixed cropping, also called intercropping, is a farming system in which two or more different crops are grown on the same piece of land at the same time during the same season. The crops are selected because they complement each other in terms of the space, light, water and nutrients they use. Mixed cropping is widespread among smallholder farmers throughout Ghana.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Makes efficient use of land by growing multiple crops simultaneously.
- If one crop fails, the other may still produce a harvest, reducing total income loss.
- Reduces weed growth because the ground is more fully covered.
- Some crop combinations reduce pest problems because different plants attract different pests.
- Can provide better household nutrition by growing multiple food types together.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Difficult to mechanise, as farm machinery cannot easily work around multiple crops.
- Harvesting is more complex when different crops are ready at different times.
- If crop combinations are poorly planned, crops may compete with each other for space and nutrients.
- Application of specific pesticides or fertilisers to one crop may affect the other.

pages.title: Mixed Farming
pages.body:
Mixed farming is a farming system in which a farmer practises both crop production and animal keeping on the same farm. The two enterprises are linked in a productive cycle: crop residues (stems, leaves, husks) feed the animals, and animal manure is returned to the land as an organic fertiliser for the crops. Mixed farming is common in the Central Region and Brong-Ahafo Region of Ghana, and among smallholder farmers across the country.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Creates a productive cycle that reduces the need to buy external fertilisers or animal feeds.
- Income comes from multiple sources (crop sales, meat, milk, eggs), reducing financial risk.
- Animal manure improves soil structure and fertility over time.
- Makes full use of all farm resources, including crop waste.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Requires more labour, skill and management than a single enterprise.
- Animals may damage crops if not properly penned or supervised.
- Higher initial cost to acquire livestock.
- Managing two enterprises simultaneously can be challenging for a single farmer.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Mixed Cropping vs Mixed Farming: a critical comparison

pages.title: Mixed Cropping vs Mixed Farming: a critical comparison
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Mixed Cropping** | **Mixed Farming** |
|---|---|---|
| What is combined? | Two or more crop species on the same land. | Crop growing and animal keeping on the same farm. |
| Animals involved? | No. Only plants are involved. | Yes. Animals are a central part of the system. |
| Key benefit | Efficient use of space and reduced crop failure risk. | Productive cycle between animals and crops. |
| Main challenge | Difficulty of mechanisation and complex harvesting. | More management skill and labour needed. |

pages.title: Pastoral Farming
pages.body:
Pastoral farming is a farming system that involves keeping and raising livestock (animals) as the primary or sole enterprise, with no crop cultivation. The farmer focuses entirely on animals such as cattle, sheep, goats, camels or horses. Pastoral farmers may be nomadic (moving with their herds to find fresh pasture) or sedentary (keeping animals on fixed pastureland). Pastoral farming is most common in the northern savanna regions of Ghana where the dry season limits crop cultivation.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Well suited to dry, semi-arid areas where crops cannot grow reliably.
- Livestock can walk to find water and pasture, making them adaptable to difficult environments.
- Provides meat, milk, hides and other animal products.
- Animals can be kept as a form of savings and sold when needed.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Mixed Farming vs Pastoral Farming: a critical comparison

pages.body:
**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- No crop production means the farmer depends entirely on animal sales and products for income.
- Nomadic pastoralism can lead to overgrazing, soil erosion and conflict over land.
- Animals are vulnerable to drought, disease and flooding.
- Yields no plant-based food for the family directly from the farm.

pages.title: Mixed Farming vs Pastoral Farming: a critical comparison
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Mixed Farming** | **Pastoral Farming** |
|---|---|---|
| Crops grown? | Yes. Crops and animals are both kept. | No. Animals only. |
| Income sources | Crops and animal products. | Animal products only. |
| Suited to | Areas with adequate rainfall for both crops and pasture. | Dry, semi-arid areas where crops are unreliable. |
| Farmer's movement | Stays on one farm. | May be nomadic or sedentary. |
| Soil management | Animal manure enriches soil for crops. | Overgrazing risk can lead to soil degradation. |

questions.q: A farmer grows maize and groundnuts on the same plot at the same time, and also keeps goats on the same farm. Which farming system(s) is this farmer practising? Explain your answer.
Explain why a pastoral farmer in northern Ghana might choose animals over crops as a main enterprise.
Compare mixed cropping and mixed farming by stating one similarity and two differences.
Explain how animal manure in mixed farming connects to what you learned about organic nutrient sources in Crop Production.

pages.body:
Think about these four questions. Does the food you eat come from a farm that uses chemicals? Is it grown to feed a family or to sell in supermarkets overseas? Is the farmer concerned only about no chemicals, or also about protecting the entire local ecosystem? Does the farmer use machinery and hired workers, or family members with hand tools?

- What is the difference between farming that is chemical-free and farming that actively tries to protect the whole ecosystem?
- What is the difference between a farmer who grows food only for their family and one who grows it for export?

pages.title: Organic Farming
pages.body:
Organic farming is a farming system that avoids all synthetic (manufactured) chemical fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides. Instead, it uses natural inputs such as compost, animal manure, green manure, and biological pest control (e.g. natural predators, neem-based sprays). Organic farming aims to produce food that is free of synthetic chemical residues, which is considered healthier for consumers and safer for the environment.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Produces food without synthetic chemical residues, which many consumers consider healthier.
- Protects soil organisms and biodiversity by avoiding chemicals that kill soil life.
- Reduces the cost of chemical inputs.
- Can access premium organic markets that pay higher prices, especially for export.
- Maintains long-term soil health better than chemical-dependent farming.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Initially produces lower yields than conventional chemical farming, especially in the first few years.
- Requires more knowledge and labour for composting and natural pest control.
- Organic certification for export markets can be expensive to obtain.
- Pest and disease control is harder without chemical pesticides.
- Composting and manure application are more laborious than applying liquid fertilisers.

pages.title: Ecological Farming
pages.body: Ecological farming (also called agroecology) is a farming approach that goes beyond the principles of organic farming. While organic farming focuses primarily on avoiding synthetic chemicals, ecological farming aims to design entire farm systems that work in harmony with natural ecosystems. It promotes biodiversity, maintains soil health, recycles nutrients, manages water sustainably, and integrates crops, trees, animals and natural habitats on the same farm. It is the broadest of all sustainable farming approaches.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Builds and maintains long-term ecosystem health across the whole farm.
- Maximises biodiversity by integrating trees, crops, animals and natural spaces.
- Resilient to climate change because diverse, healthy ecosystems recover better from stress.
- Can improve both food security and environmental conservation simultaneously.
- Reduces dependence on external inputs by cycling nutrients within the farm system.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- More complex to plan and manage than conventional farming or even organic farming.
- Requires deep knowledge of local ecology and farming science.
- Initial yields may be lower while the ecosystem is being established.
- Less familiar to farmers accustomed to conventional or simple organic methods.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Organic Farming vs Ecological Farming: a critical comparison

pages.title: Organic Farming vs Ecological Farming: a critical comparison
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Organic Farming** | **Ecological Farming** |
|---|---|---|
| Main focus | Avoiding synthetic chemicals. | Designing the whole farm to work like a healthy ecosystem. |
| Scope | Narrower: inputs (what is and is not applied). | Broader: whole farm ecology, biodiversity, water, soil and energy flows. |
| Use of trees | Not necessarily emphasised. | Often includes trees and natural habitat as integral parts of the farm. |
| Goal | Chemical-free food production. | Long-term ecological sustainability of the whole farm system. |
| All organic farms are ecological? | Not necessarily. | Ecological farms are usually also organic in their inputs. |

pages.title: Subsistence Farming
pages.body:
Subsistence farming is a farming system in which a farmer grows just enough food to feed their own family or household, with little or nothing left over to sell. The farm is small, inputs are minimal (mostly family labour and locally available organic matter), and the main goal is household food security. Subsistence farming is the most common form of farming among rural households in Ghana, particularly in the Northern, Upper East and Upper West Regions.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Provides direct food security for the household without depending on markets.
- Low cost to start and operate, as mainly family labour and local resources are used.
- Farmers grow a variety of foods that provide nutritional diversity.
- Very low debt risk, as little capital is borrowed.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- Does not generate cash income, leaving households vulnerable to poverty.
- Any crop failure leaves the family with no food and no money to buy food.
- Low productivity compared to commercial farming.
- Limits investment in education, health and other needs because there is no surplus income.
- Does not contribute significantly to the national economy through exports or taxes.

pages.title: Commercial Farming
pages.body: Commercial farming is a farming system in which crops or animals are produced primarily for sale and profit. The farm is usually large, uses modern machinery, hired labour, improved seed varieties and chemical or organic inputs. The goal is to maximise output and profit. In Ghana, examples of commercial farming include large cocoa plantations, pineapple farms for export, poultry farms, fish farms, and large-scale maize and tomato farms.

**Merits (advantages)**
- Generates significant income, supporting economic development and employment.
- Benefits from economies of scale (the larger the farm, the lower the cost per unit produced).
- Can supply large quantities of food for the national market and for export.
- Access to modern technology and improved varieties increases productivity.
- Contributes to GDP and government revenue through taxes and export earnings.

**Demerits (disadvantages)**
- High capital (money) needed to start and operate: machinery, seeds, inputs, storage.
- Heavy reliance on chemical fertilisers and pesticides can damage the environment.
- If the market price of the crop falls, the farmer may make a loss on a very large scale.
- Can displace smallholder farmers and reduce access to land for rural communities.
- Large-scale monoculture on commercial farms increases environmental risks.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Subsistence Farming vs Commercial Farming: a critical comparison

pages.title: Subsistence Farming vs Commercial Farming: a critical comparison
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Subsistence Farming** | **Commercial Farming** |
|---|---|---|
| Main purpose | Feed the farmer's own family. | Produce food for sale and profit. |
| Scale | Small (often 1–2 hectares). | Large (tens to thousands of hectares). |
| Technology used | Hand tools and family labour. | Machinery, hired workers, modern inputs. |
| Capital needed | Very low. | Very high. |
| Risk level | Crop failure means food shortage. | Crop failure or price drops mean financial loss. |
| Contribution to economy | Limited; mainly household level. | Significant; national GDP, employment, export earnings. |

questions.q: Explain, in your own words, what makes ecological farming broader than organic farming.
Describe a typical subsistence farm in a rural Ghanaian community. Include the farm size, types of crops, labour used and purpose.
Explain why commercial farming generates more income than subsistence farming, and what risks come with this.
A farmer in your community has always grown food for her family. She now wants to sell at the market. What changes would she need to make to move from subsistence to commercial farming?

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Classifying, Comparing and Evaluating Farming Systems

pages.body:
You have now studied twelve different farming systems. Some look similar on the surface but have important differences. Some can be combined. Some suit certain regions of Ghana better than others.

Before you read on, attempt this classification exercise on your own.

- Esi grows only maize on a large farm with tractors and hired workers. She sells everything.
- Kofi clears a new patch of forest every three years, burns the trees, plants cassava and then moves on.
- Akua grows tomatoes and peppers on one plot while keeping chickens. The chicken droppings go on the tomatoes.
- Mensah keeps 200 cattle across grassland in the Upper East Region and grows no crops.
- Yaa plants cowpeas after maize every season. She never plants the same crop twice in a row on the same land.

Match each farmer to a farming system. Then share your answers with a partner.

pages.title: Key to the classification exercise
pages.body: Esi = Commercial Farming (large scale, machinery, hired labour, sold for profit). Kofi = Shifting Cultivation (clears new land, burns vegetation, moves on). Akua = Mixed Farming (crops and animals on the same farm, manure used). Mensah = Pastoral Farming (livestock only, no crops). Yaa = Crop Rotation (planned sequence, same land).

pages.title: Classifying by three key questions
pages.body:
| **Question** | **If YES** | **Farming system** |
|---|---|---|
| Is only one crop grown, on large land, same crop every year? | Yes | Monoculture |
| Is only one crop grown per season (but may change next season)? | Yes | Monocropping |
| Are multiple crops grown on the same land at the same time? | Yes | Mixed Cropping |
| Are crops and animals both kept on the same farm? | Yes | Mixed Farming |
| Are animals kept with NO crops at all? | Yes | Pastoral Farming |
| Does the farmer clear brand new land and then abandon the old? | Yes | Shifting Cultivation |
| Does the farmer rotate among defined existing plots? | Yes | Land Rotation |
| Are different crops grown on the same plot in a planned sequence each season? | Yes | Crop Rotation |
| Is farming done only with natural inputs (no synthetic chemicals), focused on inputs only? | Yes | Organic Farming |
| Does the system design the whole farm to work like an ecosystem? | Yes | Ecological Farming |
| Is food grown only to feed the farmer's household? | Yes | Subsistence Farming |
| Is food grown primarily to sell for profit? | Yes | Commercial Farming |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Summary table: reasons, merits and demerits of all twelve systems

pages.title: Summary table: reasons, merits and demerits of all twelve systems
pages.body:
| **System** | **Main reason used** | **Key merit** | **Key demerit** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shifting Cultivation | Land is plentiful; no fertiliser cost needed | Soil recovers naturally; low cost | Deforestation; not suitable for populated areas |
| Land Rotation | Maintains fertility without fertilisers; stable base for farmer | Soil rests and recovers; farmer stays in one place | Requires multiple plots; land idle during fallow |
| Crop Rotation | Restores soil fertility; breaks pest cycles | Natural soil improvement via legumes; fewer pests | Requires planning; not all crops sell equally |
| Mixed Cropping | Maximises land use; reduces risk | Efficient; if one crop fails another survives | Difficult to mechanise; complex harvesting |
| Mixed Farming | Creates productive cycle of crops and animals | Manure reduces fertiliser cost; multiple income sources | More labour and management required |
| Pastoral Farming | Suited to dry areas unsuitable for crops | Adaptable livestock in difficult environments | No crop income; overgrazing risk |
| Monoculture | Maximises single-crop production at large scale | Highly efficient; easy to manage uniformly | Rapid pest build-up; high chemical dependence |
| Monocropping | Simple management; focus on one crop | Easy to apply targeted inputs; efficient harvest | No backup if crop fails; may exhaust soil |
| Organic Farming | Healthy food; reduce chemical costs; premium market | Safer food; protects soil life and biodiversity | Lower initial yields; harder pest control |
| Ecological Farming | Long-term sustainability; ecosystem health | Builds resilient, biodiverse farm systems | Complex to plan; requires specialist knowledge |
| Subsistence Farming | Household food security; low cost | Direct food supply; low debt risk | No cash income; vulnerable to crop failure |
| Commercial Farming | Profit and income generation; national supply | High productivity; employment; export earnings | High capital needed; environmental risks |

Note: In practice, a single farmer may combine more than one system. For example, a farmer can practise mixed cropping (growing maize and cassava together) using organic farming methods (no synthetic chemicals) on a subsistence basis (food for the family). These categories overlap and are not mutually exclusive.

pages.title: Farming systems in your community
pages.body: Survey the farming activities in your community. Observe or interview farmers, then classify each farm under the appropriate system or systems. Group the systems you find by the categories in this chapter and present your findings to the class.

questions.q: Classify each description under the correct farming system. (a) A farmer keeps goats only, moving between pastures in the dry season. (b) A large company grows only pineapples on 500 hectares and exports them. (c) A farmer grows maize for her family using compost but no chemicals. (d) A farmer plants cassava on Plot A this year while Plot B rests, and will swap next year.
What three questions should you ask to decide whether a farm is subsistence or commercial?
Explain why ecological farming is broader than organic farming using one example of a feature that ecological farming includes which organic farming does not necessarily.
A community in northern Ghana has very little rainfall. Which farming system or combination of systems would you recommend, and why?

pages.body:
- A farming system is an organised approach to managing a farm, covering decisions about land use, crops, animals and inputs.
- Shifting cultivation involves clearing and burning new land, farming it for a few seasons and then moving on permanently. Land rotation involves rotating among fixed, defined plots.
- Crop rotation grows different crops in a planned sequence on the same land, following principles such as including legumes, alternating root depths and never repeating the same plant family.
- Monocropping grows one crop per season; monoculture grows the same crop on large land year after year. Both differ from crop rotation and mixed cropping.
- Mixed cropping grows multiple crops on the same land at the same time. Mixed farming combines crops and animals on the same farm. Pastoral farming keeps animals only, with no crops.
- Organic farming avoids all synthetic chemicals. Ecological farming goes further and designs the whole farm to work in harmony with natural ecosystems.
- Subsistence farming produces food only for the household. Commercial farming produces food primarily for sale and profit.
- No single system suits every situation. The best choice depends on land availability, capital, rainfall, market access and the farmer's goals. Many farmers combine elements of several systems.

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Farming system | An organised method of managing a farm |
| Shifting cultivation | Clearing and burning new land, farming briefly and then moving on permanently |
| Slash-and-burn | Cutting down vegetation and burning it to clear new farmland |
| Land rotation | Rotating cultivation among defined, fixed plots while leaving others fallow |
| Fallow | Land left uncultivated to allow its fertility to recover |
| Crop rotation | Growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same land |
| Legume | A crop whose roots fix nitrogen into the soil (e.g. cowpeas, groundnuts) |
| Mixed cropping | Growing two or more crops on the same land at the same time |
| Mixed farming | Combining crop growing and animal keeping on the same farm |
| Pastoral farming | Raising livestock as the main enterprise with no crop production |
| Monoculture | Growing the same single crop on large land year after year |
| Monocropping | Growing only one crop during a season |
| Organic farming | Farming using only natural inputs with no synthetic chemicals |
| Ecological farming | Designing the whole farm to work in harmony with the natural ecosystem |
| Subsistence farming | Producing food only to feed the farmer's household |
| Commercial farming | Producing food primarily for sale and profit |

questions.q: Which of the following best describes shifting cultivation?
o: Rotating between defined plots while leaving some fallow
Growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same land
Clearing new land, farming it briefly, then permanently moving to clear more new land
Growing crops and keeping animals on the same farm

questions.q: A farmer has four plots. She farms Plot 1 this year, Plot 2 next year, Plot 3 the year after, and so on, leaving the others to rest. Which farming system is this?
What is the main ecological benefit of including a leguminous crop in a crop rotation?
o: Its roots fix nitrogen from the air into the soil
It produces the highest yield of any crop

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes monoculture from monocropping?
o: Monoculture involves rotating one crop across seasons; monocropping does not
Monoculture grows the same crop on large land year after year; monocropping grows one crop per season
Monocropping is only practised on large commercial farms
They mean exactly the same thing

questions.q: Mixed farming differs from mixed cropping in that mixed farming:
o: Grows more than one crop at the same time
Also involves keeping animals on the farm
Uses crop rotation as a core principle
Is only used on large commercial farms

questions.q: A farmer in the Upper West Region of Ghana keeps cattle and sheep and grows no crops. Which farming system is this?
Which of the following is a demerit of monoculture?
o: Pests and diseases build up rapidly because the same crop is grown every year
It requires knowledge of which crops complement each other
Yields are too low to be profitable

questions.q: What makes ecological farming broader in scope than organic farming?
o: Ecological farming allows limited use of synthetic chemicals
Ecological farming designs the whole farm to work with the natural ecosystem, not just avoiding chemicals
Organic farming grows more crop varieties than ecological farming
Ecological farming is only suitable for large commercial farms

questions.q: Which pair of farming systems are most easily confused because both involve leaving land to rest?
A smallholder farmer grows cassava, maize and garden eggs only to feed her household with no surplus for sale. This is an example of:
Which principle of crop rotation states that you should not plant maize after sorghum?
o: Follow heavy feeders with light feeders
Never plant the same crop family twice in a row
